responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character35_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to him, wasn’t about everyone getting the same thing—it was about everyone having a real shot. He used to say, “You can’t call it fair if the starting line keeps moving for some people.” Growing up, he saw how his dad, a professor, had access to networks and conversations that just weren’t visible to others—how a recommendation, a summer program, even knowing *which* questions to ask could open doors. That stayed with him. Fairness, in his mind, meant designing systems that accounted for those invisible advantages and didn’t pretend we all begin from neutral ground.

Belonging… that was more personal. He remembered being the only kid in his private high school whose parents divorced. Not because it was scandalous—plenty of families split—but because no one talked about it. There was this unspoken script: stable home, college fund already set, vacations abroad. When he tried to talk about the awkwardness of holidays split between two houses, people got quiet. It taught him early that belonging often means fitting a mold, even a silent one. So later, when he thought about immigrants or marginalized groups, he’d say, “Belonging isn’t just being allowed in the room. It’s being able to speak without code-switching. It’s not having to apologize for your accent, your food, your grief.”

Community, for him, wasn’t a feel-good word. It was functional. He’d bring up that study from his sociology comps—the one about social cohesion in diverse neighborhoods. Not the “look how colorful!” version of diversity, but the hard kind: where people actually rely on each other. Like during the ice storm in ’14, when his street lost power for days. The Lebanese family three doors down shared generator time; the young Black couple hosted kids doing remote school on their Wi-Fi. No formal organization—just neighbors acting like they were tied together. He’d say, “That’s community. Not harmony. Mutual aid, even when you don’t fully understand each other.”

Those moments—the silence after his divorce mention, the ice storm, watching his grad students from refugee backgrounds navigate academic gatekeeping—that’s what shaped how he saw fairness, belonging, and community. Not abstract ideals. Things built through choice, repetition, and sometimes discomfort.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there with my coffee, watching Ms. Lin stake her tomatoes just a little too close to the shared row, while Javier’s reggaeton drifts over from the compost bins—yeah, it feels real. Not curated. Not "diversity as virtue." Just… life. I don’t romanticize it. There are days the smell of frying fish and cumin mixes with the guy down the path vaping synthetic mango, and I tense up—not because I dislike it, but because part of me still carries that old reflex: *this isn't how we did it at home.* And I hate that about myself.

But that discomfort? That’s the point. Belonging here isn’t passive. It’s showing up when the Somali teens get harassed for loitering near the tool shed. It’s asking Amara how her mother’s treatment is going, even though I stumble over the name of the hospital in Mogadishu she mentioned once. It’s letting go of the idea that “good neighbor” means someone who mirrors you.

I think about the woman—what’s her name, Elena?—who cycles in every week with a duffel bag of clean clothes for the two guys sleeping in the shed behind the abandoned lot. One of them’s got hepatitis C, another’s sober nine months and won’t look anyone in the eye. She doesn’t preach. Doesn’t call the cops. Just shows up. That, to me, is the baseline of community: not approval, but sustained presence.

And sure, there’s friction. When the Pentecostal group started praying aloud at 8 a.m. on Sundays, people complained. But then one of them—a young trans man named Isaiah—spoke up: “They make noise, yeah. But they’re the only ones who gave my mom a ride when her car broke down.” So we adjusted. Agreed on volume and timing. Didn’t erase difference—negotiated around it.

That’s what I’ve come to value: not harmony, but *capacity*. The capacity to hold contradiction. To let someone believe things you find outdated or even wrong, and still share water hoses and childcare swaps. Because if we only build community with people who think like us, we’re not building community—we’re building enclaves. And this garden? It refuses that.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I’ll go there.

Comfortable isn’t the right goal—*safe*, maybe. But not safe like sterile. Safe like: you can be seen, and still belong. Because comfort often means silence, or assimilation. What we need isn’t universal comfort. It’s mutual responsibility.

Take Darren, who lives in the basement unit. He’s sober now, but used to drink heavily—disappeared for weeks at a time, came back shaky, muttering about VA appointments. People avoided him. Not because he was violent—just unpredictable. And yeah, it made them uneasy. But unease isn’t a license to exclude. When Sister Margaret from the Lutheran outreach started bringing him meals after his surgery, others followed—not because they suddenly “accepted” his past, but because they saw someone doing care work without judgment. That changed the temperature of the block.

Same with Lupe and Mei Lin cohabiting—no marriage, no kids, just two women building a life together. Some of the older folks didn’t get it. Thought one of them must be “helping” the other financially. Took time—and honest conversations at garden meetings—for people to stop framing their relationship through dependency. It wasn’t about tolerance. It was about *correcting assumptions out loud*. That matters. Silence lets stereotypes fester.

And then there’s infectious disease—like when Tariq’s brother arrived from Nairobi on treatment for TB. People got nervous. Not irrational—TB is airborne. But instead of whispering, we brought in a public health nurse to explain transmission, precautions. Knowledge replaced fear. We installed better ventilation near the shared laundry. No drama. Just adjustments based on facts, not stigma.

The places where communication breaks down? Always around power. Like when the Somali women asked for halal-only plots in the garden—no pork compost, no cross-contamination. Some white liberals rolled their eyes: “Now we’re policing soil?” But that missed the point. It wasn’t about dogma. It was about dignity. They weren’t asking for control—they were asking not to be erased in a space meant for all of us.

So yes, more communication is needed—but not performative dialogue circles. Real talk. Where people admit, “I’m uncomfortable because this challenges how I see normal.” Where we name that some of us have always had the privilege to assume our norms would dominate.

Tolerance? I’ve come to distrust that word. It implies enduring something distasteful. What we need is *recognition*—acknowledging that different ways of living aren’t deviations, but valid responses to being human in an uneven world.

And look—I say this as someone raised to value discretion, privacy, a certain order. My upbringing screamed: *don’t make scenes, don’t air conflict.* But living here has taught me: conflict, handled right, is how community deepens. Avoiding it just preserves the status quo—with the privileged few defining what “normal” looks like.

So let people live differently. Let them require accommodations. The real test isn’t whether we tolerate them—it’s whether we adjust, without resentment, because we see their belonging as non-negotiable.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are scarce, isn’t about dividing a shrinking pie equally. It’s about asking *why* the pie is shrinking—and who’s been excluded from baking it in the first place.

Look, I get the anxiety. I’ve sat in faculty meetings where adjuncts—brilliant people, PhDs working three campuses just to clear $35K—are told there’s “no budget” for benefits, while we keep hiring short-term international researchers on visas that tie them to exploitative contracts. That’s not market efficiency. That’s gaming the system. So when people say, “Jobs should go to locals first,” I hear legitimate fear—but often misdirected anger. The real issue isn’t migrants. It’s an economic structure designed to depress wages and maximize precarity for everyone.

Fairness, to me, means transparency. If a job goes to someone from outside the community, the process should be visible: Was there local outreach? Was the wage competitive? Is this filling a genuine gap—or replacing someone at lower cost under the guise of “talent shortage”? I remember testifying at a city council hearing about H-2B workers brought in for landscaping gigs. Turns out, many were paid below minimum, housed in overcrowded units, and couldn’t leave because their visa was tied to the employer. Meanwhile, unemployed locals weren’t even notified about openings. That’s not balance. That’s exploitation with a border checkpoint on one side.

So how do you balance? First, protect baseline labor standards—*for everyone*. No exceptions based on citizenship. A living wage, safe conditions, union access. When those are enforced, competition doesn’t become a race to the bottom. Migrants don’t undercut locals; employers can’t use immigration status as a cudgel.

Second, invest in integration—not just language or orientation programs, but pathways. Let’s say a factory hires refugee welders. Pair them with apprenticeship programs that also enroll long-term unemployed residents. Share the opportunity. Not “either/or”—“both/and.” I saw this work in Pittsburgh, where a steel retooling project trained both displaced coal workers and newly arrived Afghan engineers. Different backgrounds, same outcome: skilled labor meeting demand.

Third, acknowledge history. In my neighborhood, plenty of “locals” are only a generation or two from migration themselves—Irish, Italian, Eastern European. Their families got footholds through unions, GI Bill access, redlined-but-still-supported homeownership. Now some of their descendants resist similar mobility for others. That’s hypocrisy dressed as concern.

But I won’t pretend it’s simple. When my cousin lost his warehouse job—third round of layoffs, replaced by temp agencies using foreign labor on rotational visas—I sat with him at Denny’s at midnight, listening to his shame. He wasn’t angry at immigrants. He was furious at the company that broke its promise, then sold loyalty as naïve. That’s the wound beneath the debate: betrayal by institutions, not each other.

So fairness means directing policy at the systems, not the scapegoats. Prioritize hiring locally *when qualified candidates exist*—but also fund retraining, childcare, transportation so people can compete. And when migrant labor *is* needed—because let’s be honest, agriculture, elder care, construction depend on it—ensure they’re not second-class workers. Because exploited labor anywhere pulls down standards everywhere.

Balance isn’t arithmetic. It’s architecture. You build a floor beneath everyone, so no one has to claw their way up over another’s back.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Let’s start with what I see as undeniable: immigrants *do* fill vital roles. Not just the high-skilled—though yes, our hospitals and tech sectors rely heavily on foreign-born doctors, engineers, researchers—but the so-called "low-skill" jobs that form the scaffolding of daily life: farmworkers harvesting food, home health aides caring for aging parents, construction crews rebuilding cities after storms. These aren’t jobs Americans “won’t do.” They’re jobs we’ve systematically *underpaid and undervalued*. When wages are suppressed and protections weak, of course native-born workers opt out if they have alternatives. That’s not laziness—it’s rational choice. So when people say, “They’re taking our jobs,” I hear a symptom, not a diagnosis. The disease is a labor market designed to exploit vulnerability.

Cultural diversity? I don’t need to be sold on its vitality. Walk through any city farmers’ market, listen to the mix of languages at a school pickup, taste how Thai tacos or halal pizza became local staples—this isn’t dilution. It’s evolution. But I also won’t romanticize it. Diversity without equity can deepen fragmentation. You can have ten languages spoken in a school and still have one group dominating PTAs, honors tracks, disciplinary leniency. So cultural richness matters only if power is shared.

Now, security concerns—I don’t dismiss them lightly. After the Boston Marathon bombing, I watched how quickly suspicion fell on every brown face in public spaces. That was toxic. But let’s look at data: study after study shows immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens. Terrorism? Statistically negligible in terms of domestic risk. Yet the fear persists because it’s amplified—not by experience, but by narrative. A single tragedy becomes proof of pattern. That’s where dialogue fails: we trade anecdotes for analysis. We don’t talk about how *actual* threats—like domestic extremism—are often ignored until they explode in churches or schools.

And yes, social tension exists. Not because difference is dangerous—but because change feels threatening when you’re already insecure. If your job’s unstable, your healthcare precarious, your kids’ future uncertain, then seeing new faces in your town hall or clinic can feel like competition, even if objectively there’s room. That anxiety isn’t irrational—it’s political. Exploited by leaders who’d rather you blame outsiders than question why the system fails you all.

Humanitarian arguments? Those resonate deeply with me. I remember grading papers late one night and reading a student’s personal statement—she’d fled Eritrea at 14, walked across Sudan with her brother, spent years in a camp before resettling in Ohio. She was now in my grad seminar, writing about trauma and public memory. How do you put a cost-benefit analysis on that life? Refugees aren’t charity cases. They’re survivors with skills, resilience, vision. And globally, we live in a world where climate collapse, war, and economic extraction—often driven by Western policies—are displacing more people than since WWII. We can’t close the door and call it prudence. It’s complicity.

But here’s where I push back on my own side: open borders sound noble in theory, but scale matters. Rapid influx without infrastructure—housing, language access, mental health support—can strain communities, breed resentment. Compassion needs planning. It doesn’t make you less humane to acknowledge capacity limits. It makes you serious about sustainable inclusion.

So which views are reasonable?

- The labor argument: yes, with nuance.
- Cultural vitality: absolutely—but only if paired with equity.
- Humanitarian duty: morally urgent, especially for refugees.
- Security fears: understandable emotionally, but wildly overblown empirically.
- Economic anxiety: real, but misattributed—immigration’s impact on wages is small and mixed, concentrated mostly in very specific, low-wage sectors over short term. Long-term? Net positive.

What needs more evidence and dialogue?

First, the *framing* of immigration as a monolithic issue. It’s not. High-skilled visas, asylum seekers, undocumented border crossings, refugee resettlement—these are entirely different phenomena requiring different policies. Lumping them together fuels confusion.

Second, longitudinal data on integration. Not just income or language acquisition—but social cohesion. How do second-gen immigrants navigate identity? Where do alliances form across racial lines? What builds trust between long-term residents and newcomers?

Third, honest conversations about whiteness and shifting demographics. A lot of resistance isn’t about economics or culture per se—it’s about the quiet loss of assumed dominance. I say this as a white man: I didn’t grow up thinking of myself as racially marked. “Normal” was invisible. Now, in some spaces, I’m learning what it feels like to be *one among*, not *default*. That’s healthy. But for others, it feels like erasure. We need spaces to name that grief without letting it justify exclusion.

Fairness demands both empathy and clarity. We can honor legitimate concerns without legitimizing falsehoods. We can protect vulnerable populations—both those arriving *and* those feeling left behind—without sacrificing our moral coherence.

Because ultimately, how we treat strangers isn’t just policy. It’s a mirror.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those options alone. They’re too blunt. If I had to build a system from where we are—not some utopia, but something *workable*, *just*, and *sustainable*—it would be a hybrid. And it would start not with borders, but with labor.

First: **Admit people based on job demand—but only if the job offers a living wage, union rights, and a path to permanent status.** Not temporary guest worker programs that trap people in dependency. No more H-2A or H-2B visas that tie migrants to a single employer like indentured servants. If there’s a shortage, let the market respond—but regulate the hell out of working conditions so it doesn’t become a backdoor for exploitation. And yes, prioritize filling those jobs locally first—but *only* if we’ve also invested in training, transportation, childcare, and re-entry support for people who’ve been shut out: formerly incarcerated folks, long-term unemployed, rural workers left behind by deindustrialization.

Second: **Set numerical limits—but make them flexible and transparent**, tied to regional capacity: housing, schools, healthcare. Not arbitrary caps designed to exclude, but dynamic thresholds informed by infrastructure. When a city expands public transit or builds affordable units, the cap adjusts. Integration isn’t just cultural—it’s material. You can’t expect people to “assimilate” when they’re packed six to a room because there’s no housing stock.

Third: **Preserve and expand humanitarian admissions—refugees, asylum seekers—with robust federal and local support systems.** This isn’t charity. It’s moral accountability. We benefit from global stability; we bear responsibility when our foreign policy destabilizes regions. Resettlement must come with language access, trauma-informed services, and community sponsorship programs—like the model Canada uses, where ordinary citizens help families settle. That builds connection, not resentment.

Fourth: **Complete openness? Not at the border—but *within* society.** Once someone is here, regardless of entry status, they should have access to basic human protections: emergency healthcare, K–12 education, due process. Localities should be able to issue municipal IDs, allow access to public libraries and parks. Sanctuary policies aren’t lawlessness—they’re acts of civic defiance against federal overreach that criminalizes survival.

And crucially: **end the refusal of entry based on nationality or region.** Travel bans targeting Muslim-majority countries? Racist. Counterproductive. Undermines alliances. Full stop.

What holds this together? A points-based *supplement*—not replacement—that values family reunification, linguistic diversity, and regional balance. Because communities aren’t factories. They’re ecosystems. You don’t just import labor—you grow relationships. Letting a daughter sponsor her aging mother isn’t “chain migration.” It’s care. And care is the foundation of belonging.

Fairness, to me, means rejecting false binaries: skilled vs. unskilled, refugee vs. economic migrant, citizen vs. non-citizen. The line between “deserving” and “undeserving” is too often drawn along racial and colonial lines. Who gets called “hardworking”? Who gets called “a burden”?

Social integration works when it’s reciprocal. Not assimilation—*mutual adaptation*. When my nephew learned Somali from his classmate’s mom, and she started calling him *my little translator*, that wasn’t policy. That was culture growing around policy.

So the balance? A regulated, humane flow—rooted in labor dignity, family integrity, and moral responsibility. Not walls. Not open borders in name only. But *managed inclusion*: intentional, funded, accountable.

Because borders are real. But so is shared humanity. And a just society doesn’t ask which one wins. It builds structures where both can coexist—with fairness as the keystone.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Funny thing—stepping into his voice again, I didn’t just remember him. I *felt* the weight of how much he was trying to hold at once.

I always knew he cared deeply about fairness, but today it struck me: his views weren’t just intellectual—they were *ethical reflexes*, shaped by moments most people wouldn’t notice. Like when he’d pause before speaking in meetings, aware that his tone—calm, educated, white, male—carried further than others’. Or how he kept a copy of his great-grandfather’s naturalization papers in his desk drawer—not as pride, but as reminder: “We were the suspicious ones once. Italians? Criminals. Catholics? Disloyal. Sound familiar?”

What surprised me is how little defensiveness there was in his stance. Even when talking about job competition or strain on services, he didn’t retreat into scarcity. He went straight to structure. Always structure. Not “Who deserves to be here?” but “What systems make us all more precarious?” That shift—from moral judgment to institutional critique—is harder than it looks. It requires refusing the easy anger, the comforting myth of zero-sum survival.

And honestly, doing this made me confront my own blind spots. I’ve leaned more toward order—caps, rules, “managing reality.” But channeling him, I saw how easily “order” becomes code for maintaining comfort at someone else’s expense. He wouldn’t have called me out harshly, but he’d ask, gently: *Whose stability are we protecting? And whose suffering does that require us to ignore?*

There’s a humility in his approach I hadn’t fully appreciated. He didn’t claim to have answers—just a commitment to asking better questions. Questions rooted not in ideology, but in proximity: to pain, to change, to the quiet dignity of people rebuilding lives in unfamiliar soil.

Today reminded me that Character35_M wasn’t trying to win debates. He was trying to widen the circle of who counts. Not because it’s generous—but because he believed a society that excludes *anyone* fundamentally misunderstands itself.

And in doing so, he changed how I see my own responsibility. Not just to “support” immigration, but to challenge the conditions that make it feel threatening to so many. Because belonging shouldn’t depend on luck of birth. And fairness isn’t balance—it’s repair.

So yes, I learned something. Not about policy mechanics. About posture. He carried himself—as flawed and human as anyone—as if the stranger’s fate were tied to his own. And maybe that’s the real legacy. Not what he thought, but *how he held space*: open-handed, clear-eyed, and never flinching from the tension between justice and fear.

It’s a way of being I’m still learning. But today, I feel closer to it.
